title: Ember Consortium - Privacy, KMS, and Data Residency Solutioning
summary: Customer (Ember Consortium) wanted to validate Redwood's ability to meet strict data handling requirements: no-training guarantees, per-tenant ephemeral prompt retention, HSM-backed key management, fine-grained audit trails for e-discovery and SOC2, and SSO/RBAC mapping to their AD groups. SE ran through architecture options (hosted with VPC peering, dedicated pools, private deployment) and tradeoffs. Legal asked about exportable audit artifacts and retention windows. Next steps: send KMS integration diagram, tailored SOC2 + ISO export checklist, pilot terms, and schedule follow-up for in-depth HSM onboarding with Marco.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2028-01-12 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood CSM), Dr. Anika Sato (CISO, Ember), Marco Ruiz (Cloud Architect, Ember), Jian Li (Legal), Priya Menon (Privacy Officer)

Auto-generated sections (may be imperfect):
Summary: See metadata summary above.
Topics: KMS, HSM, no-train, prompt retention, RBAC/SSO, audit exports, data residency.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um well do a quick intro then dive into the security topics you flagged in the paperwork, Anika are you still with us?
[00:08] Dr. Anika Sato: yes sorry, yes, thanks Maya. we have about an hour fifteen, so i'll try to be succinct. main things: can you confirm no training on customer data, and how keys are handled, where audit logs live and how we can export them for legal holds.
[00:28] Maya Chen: absolutely, that's the core of today's — we want to make sure you can prove to auditors. ravi will start with the KMS/HSM flow then i'll cover retention and policy controls.
[00:38] Ravi Patel: thanks, um so at a high level Redwood supports three deployment modes that matter here: hosted with dedicated tenancy, dedicated pools, and private (VPC/on-prem). all of these can be configured with customer-managed KMS, and if you need FIPS/HSM we support HSM-backed keys via our KMS integrations. 
[00:58] Marco Ruiz: quick clarifying q — when you say "customer-managed KMS" do you mean we bring our own cloud KMS key in our account and Redwood encrypts at rest with that key? or is it like you hold a key but we have an escrow?
[01:15] Ravi Patel: good question. there are two common patterns we see: 1) bring-your-own-key where the key material never leaves your cloud KMS (we call this BYOK), we integrate via grant/role and Redwood stores data encrypted under a data key that's wrapped by your KMS key. 2) HSM-backed key in Redwood's tenant where Redwood uses an HSM (we can arrange a dedicated HSM module for a private deployment). for the strictest audit profiles we recommend BYOK + HSM in your cloud if you require full control.
[01:38] Priya Menon: and in that BYOK scenario, are you able to prove key usage logs? auditors want to see when keys were used to unwrap tokens etc.
[01:48] Ravi Patel: yes there's an audit trail — we surface KMS usage in the audit logs we ship to the customer's log sink. so you'll see grant/unwrapping events, plus our internal access logs. note sometimes cloud providers redact certain fields, so we also provide a signed metadata blob linking the unwrap to a request id.
[02:05] Jian Li: legal here — on the "signed metadata blob" is that something exportable? for e-discovery we may need chain of custody artifacts.
[02:13] Ravi Patel: yes we can provide exportable artifacts. we have an export API for audit slices; it returns a compressed bundle with timestamped events, and the signed metadata. we'll include docs in the follow-up.
[02:22] Dr. Anika Sato: okay good. next, retention — our policy is no retention of prompts beyond ephemeral session unless explicitly stored by the customer. can you confirm Redwood won't use our prompt data to train models?
[02:36] Maya Chen: short answer: yes, Redwood will not train on customer content by default. we have a strict no-training-by-default policy for customer data. there are also explicit contractual options for no training at all and prompt ephemerality — we can add a clause. 
[02:51] Marco Ruiz: how is "ephemerality" implemented? is it per-request TTL, or do you keep KV caches that could leak?
[03:01] Ravi Patel: we implement multiple layers: live KV cache for performance with configurable TTLs; optional prefix caching can be enabled or disabled per route. for customers requesting no retention, we set TTL=0 and disable cache persistence; logs still exist in transit but can be redacted. in private deployments you can also opt to store the KV cache in customer-managed volumes that you scrub.
[03:23] Priya Menon: what about system prompts or automated debugging traces? sometimes logs have request payloads for debugging. we need guarantee those are redacted or excluded.
[03:32] Ravi Patel: yes, we have redaction policies and can rotate/log-scrubbing pipelines. by default, debug traces do not contain full prompt content unless you opt in via debug mode; if you do opt-in, the traces are stored encrypted and can be time-limited.
[03:48] Dr. Anika Sato: on the SOC 2 side, do you map RBAC to our SAML groups? we need fine-grained separation so our engineers can't see other tenants' traces during incident response.
[03:58] Maya Chen: absolutely, we integrate with SAML/SSO and can map SAML assertions to RBAC roles. ravi, do you want to walk through an example?
[04:05] Ravi Patel: yeah. so you can map SAML attributes to Redwood roles — "redwood-admin", "redwood-audit", "redwood-developer" — and then assign least-privilege policies. during an incident you can create ephemeral support roles with scoping to only specific tenant ids; every elevation is logged.
[04:23] Marco Ruiz: is there an approval workflow? our ops team requires two-person approval for role elevation.
[04:28] Ravi Patel: we support approval hooks — either via an API or pre-built integrations with PagerDuty/Jira to require approvals. we also emit explicit approval events in the audit log.
[04:40] [crosstalk] Maya Chen: and for audit retention lengths — you mentioned exportable slices — what are the typical retention windows?
[04:48] Ravi Patel: default logs retention is 90 days; for enterprise we support 7+ years if required, via configurable retention and long-term storage exports to your S3, or to our long-term archival storage in a dedicated region.
[04:59] Jian Li: for GDPR and DSARs, if a user requests deletion, how do you ensure third-party backups or archival exports are also purged?
[05:09] Ravi Patel: we have a deletion workflow that issues masked deletions and tombstones; for exports to customer sinks, deletion is the customer's responsibility, but we provide a deletion marker and an export manifest so you can reconcile. for our own archival store we can run deletions on request and provide deletion certificates.
[05:25] Priya Menon: can you give an example of the deletion certificate? what does it look like?
[05:30] Maya Chen: it's a signed statement with timestamps, object ids, the retention policy run id, and who authorized the deletion. we include hashes and we can sign with our key. we'll include a sample in the packet.
[05:41] Dr. Anika Sato: the auditors are picky about chain-of-custody. do you support immutable storage for logs (WORM)?
[05:49] Ravi Patel: yes, WORM-style retention is supported in our archival tier. the logs are versioned, write-once policy in the archival bucket if you enable that.
[05:58] Marco Ruiz: one more: data residency — our EU teams must keep data in eu-west-1. can Redwood pin inference and logs to specific regions?
[06:07] Maya Chen: yes, region pinning is supported. for Hosted we can route requests to model instances in eu-west-1 and ensure logs land in your EU log sink. For Private deployments you can deploy entirely in your region.
[06:21] Marco Ruiz: cool. do you support cross-region replication for DR while keeping primary residency? auditors want to see failover plans without violating residency.
[06:30] Ravi Patel: we support controlled cross-region DR with data-at-rest encryption using separate keys per region and transcripts masked unless unmasked under emergency procedures which we document. replication can be configured as metadata-only, or full copy with explicit retention rules.
[06:44] Priya Menon: let's discuss e-discovery. we need exportable transcripts for legal holds that include user ids, timestamps, request ids, and the unwrap proof for keys. is that all available?
[06:55] Ravi Patel: yes, those fields are captured. the export package includes request_id <-> key-usage evidence, and the log lines with user IDs and any redaction markers. if you need native PDF-friendly packages for legal, we can generate that as well.
[07:06] Jian Li: what about test/dev environments? we don't want PII flowing into sandbox. how do you prevent production creds being used in dev?
[07:14] Ravi Patel: we recommend separate orgs for prod and dev, distinct API keys and network controls. we also offer a "safe playground" with synthetic data and a content filter that automatically strips PII from test runs.
[07:27] Dr. Anika Sato: can that filter be tuned for PHI specifically? healthcare terms often slip through.
[07:33] Ravi Patel: yes, we have PHI-specific redaction modules and PII/PHI recognition models you can enable on the route. they operate pre-ingest and can either reject or mask tokens.
[07:46] Marco Ruiz: latency tradeoffs — does enabling PII redaction or HSM unwrap add measurable latency? our SLA is p95 < 150ms for inference.
[07:55] Ravi Patel: good point — HSM unwraps add a small constant (tens of ms) on first-key unwrap; after that a data-key is cached with strict TTL. PII redaction adds model-invocation overhead if done via a model, but we also provide a native regex/heuristics pipeline which is faster. with proper sizing we maintain p95 < 150ms in dedicated pools, but we should load-test with your payloads.
[08:17] Maya Chen: that suggests a follow-up benchmark. Marco, would you like Redwood to run a 48-hour pilot to measure p95 and KMS unwrap latency with your specific prompts?
[08:25] Marco Ruiz: yes, that would be helpful. include a scenario with PHI redaction on.
[08:30] Maya Chen: great, we'll propose pilot scope.
[08:33] [long pause, papers shuffling]
[09:05] Priya Menon: question on contractual no-train language — is that a default or we need to buy that?
[09:12] Maya Chen: we have a default no-training-by-default policy, but for contractual assurances we offer a no-training contractual addendum (it's common in enterprise plans). that addendum explicitly prohibits Redwood from using your data for model improvement.
[09:24] Jian Li: how do you prove that during an audit?
[09:27] Ravi Patel: we provide configuration snapshots showing training flags are off, plus artifact logs showing no internal training jobs referenced customer data. for additional assurance we can also provide access to model-growth logs that show no customer data ingestion; some customers add on periodic third-party attestations.
[09:42] Dr. Anika Sato: for SSO we need SCIM provisioning mapping to our AD groups, and we want automatic deprovisioning. does Redwood support SCIM?
[09:50] Maya Chen: yes SCIM is supported. you can map groups to roles and deprovisioning is immediate; we can also run a soft-delete grace period if you prefer.
[09:59] Marco Ruiz: will deprovisioning scrub all access tokens and API keys issued to that user?
[10:04] Ravi Patel: yes. when a user is deprovisioned we revoke sessions and rotate any dependent tokens; there's an audit event for each rotation.
[10:12] Priya Menon: another auditor request: ability to run on-demand attestation that key material hasn't left the customer's HSM. can you provide attestation logs?
[10:21] Ravi Patel: for BYOK we provide provider attestation plus our own signed audit bundles. if you require, we can schedule an HSM onboarding call with our infra team to show the attestation chain.
[10:33] Maya Chen: sounds like a good follow-up — Marco, we should loop in your infra folks and our infra lead.
[10:38] Marco Ruiz: yes please.
[10:40] [brief silence]
[10:50] Jian Li: legal final question: exportability of contracts and the security docs — can you give a single compressed package with SOC2 report, ISO cert, and pen test?
[11:00] Maya Chen: yes we have a compliance pack for customers with an NDA/portal link. we'll package SOC2 Type II report redacted as needed, ISO certificate, most recent pentest exec summary, and our security architecture whitepaper.
[11:12] Priya Menon: nice. please include a summary table of control ownership between Ember and Redwood. that's crucial for our shared responsibility matrix.
[11:19] Maya Chen: will do.
[11:22] [crosstalk]
[11:30] Ravi Patel: quick note on monitoring: our console emits per-route cost and latency breakdowns, and you can hook that to your observability. we also emit structured traces that include request_id and tenant_id for traceability.
[11:44] Marco Ruiz: perfect.
[11:47] Maya Chen: ok wrapping up, let me recap next steps — i'll say them and then lena will capture action items.
[11:54] Maya Chen: 1) We'll send a tailored KMS integration diagram and sample deletion certificate. 2) We'll attach the compliance pack (SOC2, ISO, pentest summary). 3) We'll propose a 48-hour pilot scope with PHI redaction + HSM unwrap measurements. 4) Schedule HSM onboarding call with your infra and our infra lead. 5) Provide export samples for legal hold artifacts.
[12:18] Lena Ortiz: action items — captured:
- Maya Chen: send KMS integration diagram and deletion certificate sample by 2028-01-17
- Ravi Patel: produce pilot plan and measurement matrix by 2028-01-18
- Lena Ortiz: upload compliance pack to secure portal and share link by 2028-01-15
- Marco Ruiz & Redwood infra: schedule HSM onboarding meeting (target week of 2028-01-22)
- Jian Li: provide list of required fields for e-discovery export by 2028-01-16

[12:55] Dr. Anika Sato: thanks all, that covers our questions for now. we'll review the materials and follow up on the pilot.
[13:05] Maya Chen: great — thank you for the time. we'll follow up in writing with the packet and pilot proposal.
[13:12] Meeting end.
